title: Computable PAC learning versus effective sample bounds
formal: Does there exist a nonempty class \(H\) of total computable Boolean functions on \(\mathbb N\) that is properly computably PAC learnable, but not properly strongly computably PAC learnable? Precisely, require a total computable proper learner \(A\) and some function \(m_A:\mathbb N_{\ge2}^2\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), not required to be computable, such that for every \(a,b\ge2\), every sample size \(n\ge m_A(a,b)\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\mathbb N\times\{0,1\}\), \[\Pr_{S\sim D^n}\left[L_D(h_{A(S)})>\inf_{h\in H}L_D(h)+\frac1a\right]\le\frac1b.\] At the same time, require that there be no total computable proper learner \(B\) and total computable function \(m_B\) satisfying the same guarantee. Here \(h_{A(S)}\) is the computable hypothesis encoded by the learner’s output. This is the source’s Question 1 in its proper, agnostic model; the historical answer is yes.

source_formulation.text: Is there a hypothesis class that is properly computably PAC learnable but not properly strongly computably PAC learnable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: An algorithm can eventually learn with any prescribed accuracy even when no algorithm can bound how much data will suffice. The separation shows that effective prediction and effective control of sample requirements are different demands. Properness is essential: allowing a computable predictor outside the chosen class changes the answer.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Delle Rose–Kozachinskiy–Rojas–Steifer, COLT 2023, Theorem 14: a decidable class of finitely supported hypotheses is properly CPAC learnable but not properly SCPAC learnable. This matches Sterkenburg 2022 Question 1 and its proper agnostic definitions. The potentially improper notions instead coincide by the 2023 Theorem 11. The checked resolution is mathematical; no Lean formalization is asserted.

progress.text: Sterkenburg defines strong computable PAC learning, characterizes its proper version, and explicitly asks for a proper CPAC class that is not properly SCPAC learnable.
Delle Rose and coauthors answer the question affirmatively in Theorem 14, even with decidable finitely supported hypotheses and VC dimension at most three.
Their Theorem 11 separately yields equivalence of the two notions for improper learning, with the naming convention explained in Remark 6.

Checked the original proper agnostic definitions, the full theorem statement and relevant proof guarantees. Completed and archived the resolved question with explicit sample-bound and output quantifiers.

importance.reason: A foundational separation between computable learning and computable control of sample complexity. Its importance is conceptual and model-theoretic rather than an efficient algorithmic improvement; the proper/improper distinction is mathematically decisive.

sentences: A computable learner can process every finite sample and return a total computable predictor from a prescribed class.
The question asks whether such a proper learner can succeed eventually without any proper learner having a computable bound on the required sample size.
COLT 2023 answers yes, even for a decidable class of finitely supported hypotheses of small VC dimension.
The same equivalence question has the opposite answer when predictors outside the class are allowed, so the source’s proper convention is essential.
The card is archived with the matching separation theorem and its precise computational and statistical model.

definitions: Fix an ordinary effective encoding of finite sequences of natural-number/bit pairs and a standard enumeration \((\varphi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of partial Turing-computable functions. A total computable Boolean function halts on every natural input and returns 0 or 1. A learner is a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite labeled sample \(S\), including unrealizable samples, and outputs an index \(e\) such that \(h_e=\varphi_e\) is total and Boolean. Properness requires \(h_e\in H\) for every sample. This is a semantic requirement on the output, not a requirement that the learner decide totality or class membership of arbitrary program indices. The learner receives only the sample; \(a,b,D\) are not inputs. The class and learner may be fixed in advance, with no uniform algorithm over all classes requested. For a distribution \(D\), \[L_D(h)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb N}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}D(x,y)\,\mathbf1\{h(x)\ne y\}\] is the zero-one risk. All distributions are allowed, including noncomputable ones; the countable domain carries all subsets. \(S\sim D^n\) denotes \(n\) independent labeled draws. Samples may repeat points or contain contradictory labels, and no target-in-class or realizability promise is made. The only probability in the guarantee comes from this sampling; the learner itself is deterministic. The comparator uses an infimum, so existence of a risk-minimizing hypothesis is not assumed. Computably PAC learnable means that such a learner has a finite distribution-free sample threshold for every accuracy/confidence pair. Strongly computably PAC learnable additionally requires some total computable upper-bound function for those thresholds. The negative strong requirement quantifies over every candidate learner, not just the one witnessing ordinary computable learnability. No running-time or polynomial bound is imposed on either the learner or the sample-bound computation. Two integer parameters and a non-strict failure inequality are an equivalent normalization of the source’s rational accuracy/confidence conventions; doubling indices converts strict failure bounds, and replacing a pair by its maximum converts the 2023 single-index convention. No decidable or enumerable representation of \(H\) is required by the original question.
answer_criterion: A Lean completion must prove existence of a class and proper computable learner with the displayed guarantee, and prove that every proper computable learner fails to have any total computable sample bound for that class. Alternatively, a negative answer would prove that every properly computably PAC learnable class admits some proper computable learner with a computable bound. Showing only that one chosen learner has a bad bound is insufficient. So is a separation restricted to running time or polynomial sample bounds: the quantifier excludes every total computable sample bound, however fast it grows. Allowing improper output changes the question. The archived record reports a checked theorem matching the positive answer, without claiming an existing Lean formalization of its proof.

context_blocks.text: Classical PAC learning asks whether sufficiently many independent examples let a learner compete with the best hypothesis. It does not automatically supply an implementable learner or a computable threshold for sufficient data. The source separates those two effectiveness requirements while allowing arbitrary computation time.

The source uses CPAC without a qualifier for proper agnostic learning. Its explicit Question 1 asks whether the added computability requirement on sample thresholds changes learnability. The 2023 paper uses unqualified CPAC for potentially improper learners and explicitly warns about that naming difference. Reading the acronyms alone would therefore invert the apparent answer.

COLT 2023 Theorem 14 constructs a class that admits a proper computable learner but no proper strongly computable learner. The class consists of finitely supported Boolean functions and is decidable when a function is presented by its finite support. Its proof gives VC dimension at most three. Thus the separation does not depend on allowing noncomputable target functions or high statistical dimension.

Decidability of that example means deciding membership from an explicitly supplied finite set of positive inputs. It does not mean deciding whether an arbitrary Turing program computes a member of the class. The theorem and the card use ordinary program indices for the learner’s output, with totality and properness guaranteed by the learner’s specification.

For proper learning, a computable sample threshold is tied to the existence of a computable empirical-risk minimizer: a rule choosing a class member with the fewest errors on any finite sample. Computable learnability alone instead corresponds to an asymptotic version whose excess training error tends to zero without an effective rate. These are established characterizations, not additional premises of the question.

The same 2023 paper proves that if improper computable learning is possible, a computable sample bound is possible as well, using a suitable computably learnable superclass. That equivalence concerns unrestricted output hypotheses. It neither contradicts nor replaces the source’s proper separation.
